verses.text: Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken.
Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.
Abraham called his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac.
Abraham circumcised his son, Isaac, when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.
Abraham was one hundred years old when his son, Isaac, was born to him.
Sarah said, “God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.”
She said, “Who would have said to Abraham, that Sarah would nurse children? For I have borne him a son in his old age.”
The child grew, and was weaned. Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned.
Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, mocking.
Therefore she said to Abraham, “Cast out this servant and her son! For the son of this servant will not be heir with my son, Isaac.”
The thing was very grievous in Abraham’s sight on account of his son.

God said to Abraham, “Don’t let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your servant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice. For your offspring  will be accounted as from Isaac.
I will also make a nation of the son of the servant, because he is your child .”

Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread and a bottle of water, and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder; and gave her the child, and sent her away. She departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
The water in the bottle was spent, and she cast the child under one of the shrubs.
She went and sat down opposite him, a good way off, about a bow shot away. For she said, “Don’t let me see the death of the child.” She sat over against him, and lifted up her voice, and wept.
God heard the voice of the boy. The angel of God called to Hagar out of the sky, and said to her, “What ails you, Hagar? Don’t be afraid. For God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
Get up, lift up the boy, and hold him in your hand. For I will make him a great nation.”
God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the bottle with water, and gave the boy drink.
God was with the boy, and he grew. He lived in the wilderness, and became, as he grew up, an archer.
He lived in the wilderness of Paran. His mother took a wife for him out of the land of Egypt.
At that time, Abimelech and Phicol the captain of his army spoke to Abraham, saying, “God is with you in all that you do.

Now, therefore, swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me, nor with my son, nor with my son’s son. But according to the kindness that I have done to you, you shall do to me, and to the land in which you have lived as a foreigner.”
Abraham said, “I will swear.”
Abraham complained to Abimelech because of a water well, which Abimelech’s servants had violently taken away.
Abimelech said, “I don’t know who has done this thing. You didn’t tell me, and I didn’t hear of it until today.”
Abraham took sheep and cattle, and gave them to Abimelech. Those two made a covenant.
Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves.
Abimelech said to Abraham, “What do these seven ewe lambs which you have set by themselves mean?”
He said, “You shall take these seven ewe lambs from my hand, that it may be a witness to me, that I have dug this well.”
Therefore he called that place Beersheba,  because they both swore there.
So they made a covenant at Beersheba. Abimelech rose up with Phicol, the captain of his army, and they returned into the land of the Philistines.
Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and called there on the name of Yahweh, the Everlasting God.
Abraham lived as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines many days.

footnotes.content: I have learned to look for the Lord in timing. He visited Sarah just as He said He would, and when He visits, His word becomes action. Before the baby is in her arms, the faithfulness that began long ago is catching up to her again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How gentle of the Lord that the birth came 'at the set time' He had spoken. After years of waiting, grace is not rushed. I think of how the greatest set time was when the Word became flesh for those who had long waited, just as surely as He keeps His word to Sarah.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham obeys in naming what God has given. He does not call the child by some family name of his own longing, but by the name God directed: Isaac, 'laughter'. I want to learn to name the mercies of God by the joy He Himself put into them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Faithfulness shows up in small obedience. At eight days, Abraham circumcised Isaac, doing exactly what God had commanded. No delay, no bargaining. I am grateful that our greater Abraham, Jesus, was also faithful to the covenant for us, even when obedience cost Him everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hundred years old to hold the promise in his arms. It humbles me to see how slowly God often gives what He so freely promises. The older I get, the more I rest in the fact that with the Lord, delayed is never denied; it is prepared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sarah says God has made her laugh. Once she laughed in disbelief (Genesis 18:12), now she laughs in wonder. The God who humbles our doubt is also the God who turns our laughter to worship when He keeps His word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who would have said it? Sarah marvels at what only God could do. I have found that the mercies I am most grateful for are the ones I never would have dared to ask for, yet the Lord gave them out of His own kindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A great feast for a weaned child. Abraham does not hide his joy; he makes room to celebrate God's faithfulness. After so many altars of sacrifice, here is an altar of thanksgiving, and I want to learn to feast in gratitude when the Lord answers prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joy can be complicated. While Isaac is celebrated, Ishmael is mocking. Sin has a way of spoiling what grace gives. I need to watch my own heart in days of rejoicing, lest I grieve a brother or belittle what God has done for another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sarah sees clearly what must be done for the sake of the promise. The heir of the covenant cannot share the same household as one who scorns the heir. Paul later uses this to show that we are children not of the slave woman, but of the free woman by promise (Galatians 4:21-31).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham is pained. He loves Ishmael, and sending him away breaks his fatherly heart. The Lord does not rebuke his tenderness; He speaks to it. Even when obedience is right, it can still grieve us, and our God is gentle with fathers who ache.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord tells Abraham to listen to Sarah in this matter, for it is through Isaac that the offspring shall be named. God is committed to the line He chose for the sake of the One who would come. Our hope rests not on our schemes, but on the Seed promised to Abraham (Genesis 3:15; Galatians 3:8, 16).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Though Ishmael is sent away from the tent of the promise, he is not cast off by God. Because he is Abraham's child, the Lord will make him a nation. I take comfort that the God who keeps covenant with His chosen people also shows mercy to those outside in ways only He sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham rises early, gives bread and water, and sends them away with a heavy heart. He provides what little he can for the wilderness. I think of our heavenly Father who, when we are sent out with nothing, has already ordained springs of water for those He cares for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The bottle runs dry. So often God's people come to the end of their own strength in the place where only His mercy remains. It is there, with no more human provision, that we learn to look up to the God who never runs dry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hagar cannot bear to watch the boy die. She puts distance between them and weeps. The Lord sees tears that are hidden from men. Before any well appears, there is a God in heaven who hears the cry of the forsaken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God hears the voice of the boy. The angel of the Lord calls to Hagar from heaven, tenderly asking, 'What ails you, Hagar?' Our God knows our afflictions and draws near to speak comfort to those who think they are alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord gives Hagar strength for her calling: lift up the boy, hold him in your hand. He has not forgotten the promise He made to make Ishmael a great nation. The God who calls us to act in faith is the same God who gives the strength to do it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God opens her eyes, and she sees a well of water. The well was there all along, but her grief had blinded her to the mercy of God. How often the Lord opens the eyes of faith to see that He has been providing for us while we were weeping.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God was with the boy. That simple phrase is precious. In the wilderness, far from the tents of Abraham, the God of covenant mercy is present with Ishmael. The Lord is near to all who are in need, and His care reaches places we might not expect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael grows up in the wilderness of Paran, an archer, and his mother finds him a wife from Egypt. The Lord is faithful to His word to make him a nation. Even those who walk outside the line of the chosen Seed are not forgotten by the God who made all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech sees it: God is with Abraham in all that he does. A pagan king recognizes the blessing of the God of Israel. I pray that those around us would see the peace and faithfulness of our God in our lives, not for our glory, but pointing to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech asks for an oath of kindness across generations. The world knows it needs covenant faithfulness, even if it only sees it dimly. How much more those who know the faithful God should be men and women of our word, keeping covenant love for the sake of Jesus who has kept covenant for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham simply says, 'I will swear.' A man of faith keeps his word. Our Lord Jesus is the Yes and Amen to all God's promises (2 Corinthians 1:20). Because He is faithful, we can be faithful in the small things of our calling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham brings up a water well that was violently taken. Even godly men must deal with injustice in this world. He does not take vengeance; he brings it to the king and appeals for what is right. We can commit our wrongs to the Judge of all the earth, who does right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech pleads ignorance. Many disputes would be healed if we listened first. Abraham had every right to be angry, but he takes the path of peaceable negotiation. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and open to reason (James 3:17).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gifts are exchanged, and a covenant is made between two men from different nations. The God who called Abraham out is also the one making peace between Abraham and Abimelech. One day, through Abraham's Seed, people from every tribe and nation will be reconciled to God and to one another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham sets seven ewe lambs apart by themselves. He is intentional about making this matter unmistakable. A small act of clarity can prevent future strife. I want to be careful with my words and deeds so that the truth is plain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abimelech asks for meaning. Abraham is not content to assume understanding; he explains. Good covenant love speaks plainly. Our Lord explains the things of God to us, opening our eyes to see that the blessings we receive are gifts secured by His faithful love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lambs are a witness that Abraham dug this well. In a land where wells meant life, this was no small thing. The God who gave the land will also provide the water. Ultimately, our well of life is Jesus Himself, of whom anyone who drinks will never thirst again (John 4:13-14).
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They call the place Beersheba, 'Well of the Seven' or 'Well of the Oath'. This spot becomes a place of testimony between Abraham and Abimelech. Many years later, Jacob will also pass through Beersheba (Genesis 46:1-5), and the Lord will speak to him there, showing the faithfulness of God across generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The covenant is made at Beersheba. After hard words over a well, peace is restored. I have learned that reconciliation, though it may cost us something, is a precious gift. Jesus is our peacemaker, reconciling enemies to God and to one another through His cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham plants a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and calls on the name of Yahweh, the Everlasting God. A tree takes years to grow, yet he plants it as an act of worship. In the land of promise, he marks his faith in the God who is from everlasting to everlasting, the same God who has called us to hope in Christ before all worlds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: Abraham lived as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines many days. As of 2026-10, we too are sojourners and exiles in this world (1 Peter 2:11). Our true home is not here; we look for the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
